title: The SGPC, 1920
hook: Sikhs formed a committee to manage gurdwaras and a volunteer band, the Akali Dal

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Singh: an honest mind, honored by believers and doubters alike. Today, back to the gurdwaras, where the outrage over the robe turns into a plan.

Four letters on signboards and letterheads in Punjab: S, G, P, C. You can pass them without a second look. Behind them is a long name, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, and behind the long name is a question Sikhs had been asking since the robe was given to the general. Who should look after the gurdwaras? In 1920, at a gathering in Amritsar, Sikhs gave their answer. We will.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS ON SIGNBOARDS.` → `A LONG NAME BEHIND THEM.` → `WHO LOOKS AFTER THE GURDWARAS?`

segments.voice: Gurdwaras were then often in the hands of mahants, hereditary custodians, and some treated the shrines and their lands as private property. Reformers said practices had crept in that went against the Gurus' teaching, and at the Golden Temple the manager answered to the government. In 1920 Sikhs met in Amritsar and formed a committee to manage the gurdwaras on behalf of the Panth, the whole Sikh community. Its long name means, roughly, the chief committee for managing the gurdwaras. Alongside it came a band of volunteers, the Akali Dal. Akali comes from Akal, the Timeless One, a name for God. The Akalis weren't paid soldiers. They were farmers, teachers, former servicemen and students who gave their time, and later their bodies, to the work. Guru Nanak says at Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib that if you serve in this world, you'll be given a seat in the court of the Lord. The reform movement was political, and the SGPC later became a powerful elected body. But at the start it ran on seva: ordinary people taking on a job no one was paying them for.
screen: `SHRINES TREATED AS PRIVATE PROPERTY.` · `A COMMITTEE FOR THE WHOLE PANTH.` · `AKALIS: VOLUNTEERS OF THE TIMELESS.` · `SERVE IN THIS WORLD.` · then, large: `VOLUNTEERS STEPPED UP.`

segments.voice: Think of the places you belong to, a home, a workplace, a street, a gurdwara, and the one job in them nobody wants: the dishes after the meal, the chairs after the meeting. Picture yourself quietly doing it, with no one asking, and breathe slowly with that picture. Waheguru on the breath out, if you pray.
The SGPC. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, formed by Sikhs to manage their gurdwaras, with a volunteer band, the Akali Dal, beside it. Today's word.
Your line: volunteers stepped up. Nobody paid them, and they came anyway. Day nine hundred eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: The SGPC today manages historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring regions, including the Golden Temple; Sikhs also do seva in gurdwaras everywhere as volunteers, in the kitchen, cleaning and looking after shoes.
